summaries.example: Imagine a robot helping you get to school. It knows that buses usually follow routes, that a closed road may stop a trip, and that turning left changes where it is. Logic can help represent these facts and work out a plan. But the robot must also handle surprises, such as a missing bus. This shows why everyday reasoning is harder than a simple math proof.
summaries.summary: Logic-based artificial intelligence uses ideas from logic to help computers represent knowledge and reason. The goal is not only to prove simple statements, but also to handle practical problems: making plans, predicting what actions will do, explaining causes, reasoning about space, and considering what other agents know or believe. A separate knowledge representation can store general facts so that many parts of a system can use and explain them. This makes programs easier to change than systems whose knowledge is mixed into many individual procedures. Everyday reasoning is difficult because people usually ignore unlikely possibilities and expect many things to remain unchanged. Such reasoning is nonmonotonic: a new fact can cancel an earlier conclusion. Researchers have developed several logical approaches, including default reasoning, preferred-model methods, and causal theories. They also study problems such as the frame problem, which asks how to represent the things an action does not change. Philosophical logic helped begin this work, but AI applications introduced new concerns about scale, computation, testing, and usefulness. The entry presents logic in AI as both a source of practical tools and a way to develop new ideas about reasoning.
key_ideas: Logic can help computers represent knowledge and reason about actions, time, places, causes, and what other agents know.
A logical idea may inspire a program, while problems in a working program may lead researchers to improve the logic.
Everyday reasoning often uses assumptions about what normally happens. These assumptions can be withdrawn when new facts arrive.
A major challenge is deciding what stays the same after an action. This is called the frame problem.
Logic-based AI grew from philosophical logic but developed new methods because computer systems must work with large bodies of information and real applications.
summaries.why_it_matters: Logic-based AI matters because intelligent behavior requires more than storing isolated facts. A system needs to connect information, make plans, notice exceptions, and sometimes explain its conclusions. Studying these tasks can improve computer programs and also teach us about reasoning itself. The field shows that simple-looking common sense can become a serious challenge when we try to make it precise and usable.

important_terms.definition: A way of representing facts and rules so a computer can use them to draw conclusions.
The study and design of computer programs that can behave in ways we call intelligent.
Information stated as facts, rather than hidden inside a step-by-step procedure.
Reasoning that can change when new information or an exception appears.
A computer’s search for a series of actions that reaches a goal.

questions_to_think_about: When should a computer assume that something has stayed the same?
Why might a plan that is reasonable still fail?
Is a computer’s answer easier to trust if it can explain the facts and rules behind it?
Can everyday common sense be written as a complete set of rules?

summaries.example: Suppose a planning system is told that a pistol is unloaded, a turkey is alive, and the system can load, wait, and shoot. A natural rule says that facts normally persist unless an action changes them. After loading and waiting, however, a naive default theory may allow the gun to become unloaded for no stated reason. Then shooting need not make the turkey no longer alive. This is the Yale Shooting Anomaly: a formalism that seems to capture inertia can still produce an implausible plan result.
summaries.summary: The entry examines how logic is used to understand and build AI systems that reason about intelligent action. Logic may specify what a program should compute, or it may simply influence design; in either case, implementations can expose weaknesses in existing theories and motivate new ones. Knowledge representation emerged as an important way to keep general declarative information separate from procedures that use it, making systems more modular and potentially more explainable. The central philosophical contrast is between mathematical, monotonic consequence and practical, nonmonotonic reasoning. In ordinary planning, agents ignore remote possibilities, rely on normal expectations, and revise conclusions when exceptions appear. Nonmonotonic approaches include circumscription and other preferential methods, default logic, modal or autoepistemic theories, and causal accounts. These approaches differ in whether they select preferred models or allow multiple extensions—alternative coherent consequence sets. Logic-based AI also formalizes action and change. In situation-calculus-style systems, actions transform situations, and planning searches for an action sequence that reaches a goal. The frame problem concerns the persistence of properties; related qualification and ramification problems concern exceptions, failed actions, and indirect effects. The Yale Shooting Anomaly demonstrates that a plausible inertia rule can produce an unintended result, so successful formalisms must be tested across many benchmark scenarios. The entry also surveys causal, spatial, epistemic, taxonomic, contextual, and practical reasoning, presenting AI as both an application domain for philosophical logic and a source of distinctive logical innovations.
key_ideas: Logical AI began under the influence of philosophical logic, especially the project of formalizing practical common-sense reasoning, but its application to large computational systems generated new theories.
The connection between logic and programs can be strict, as when soundness and completeness are proved, or looser, when logical ideas merely guide part of a system’s design.
Knowledge representation separates reusable declarative information from reasoning procedures. This supports maintenance, multiple uses, and explanations.

Classical consequence is monotonic: adding premises cannot remove an existing consequence. Commonsense reasoning is often nonmonotonic because defaults depend on normality, limited attention, or the absence of contrary information.

Planning formalizations represent states, actions, preconditions, effects, and goals. They must address inertia, unsuccessful actions, indirect effects, incomplete information, and sometimes concurrent actions.
Philosophical logic and logical AI still share a concern with reasoning, but AI places stronger emphasis on feasible implementation, algorithmic analysis, large knowledge bases, and applications.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic matters because reasoning systems must operate with incomplete, changing, and structured information rather than with isolated textbook premises. Formalization makes hidden assumptions visible: what counts as normal, what persists, what causes an effect, and how exceptions are handled. These questions affect planning, robotics, knowledge bases, and systems that reason about other agents. They also reveal limits of purely abstract theories and show how computational applications can reshape philosophical questions about rational reasoning.

important_terms.definition: A formal system for analyzing which conclusions follow from stated premises.
The AI subfield concerned with programs whose behavior can broadly be described as intelligent.
A representation of facts and other information that is kept distinct from procedures for using it.
A consequence relation in which adding information can defeat a conclusion that was previously supported.
A rule that licenses a conclusion when supporting information is present and blocking information is absent.
A framework in which actions transform situations, allowing a system to describe their effects and plan sequences.
The challenge of representing why most relevant properties remain unchanged after an action, while allowing genuine changes.
A theory in which preferred interpretations are selected by minimizing or otherwise favoring certain possibilities.

questions_to_think_about: Should a theory of commonsense reasoning use defaults, probabilities, or both for different tasks?
What is lost when a practical planning problem is treated like a proof?
How should a formal system distinguish an action that cannot be attempted from one that is attempted but fails?
Does a theory need one unique set of conclusions, or can several extensions represent unresolved alternatives?
What standards should determine whether a formalization is faithful to common sense?

summaries.example: A school-planning app knows that Maya usually walks home after practice. It may infer that she will walk today. Then it learns that there is a storm and the school has closed the path. The app should withdraw its first conclusion and choose another route. This is different from ordinary mathematical proof, where adding another true fact does not erase an earlier consequence. The app needs a default rule about what normally happens and a way to handle exceptions.
summaries.summary: Logic-based artificial intelligence studies how formal reasoning can help computers act intelligently. Its roots lie partly in philosophical logic, but the problems of building useful systems have pushed the field toward knowledge representation, automated reasoning, and computationally testable theories. Logic can provide a precise specification for a program, although a program may also use logical ideas more informally. In either case, real applications can reveal gaps in a theory and encourage new research. A central aim associated with early logical AI was to formalize common sense: the reasoning used in planning, understanding stories, diagnosing devices, reasoning about physical objects, and thinking about other agents’ beliefs or goals. This reasoning is not like a complete mathematical proof. People normally ignore many unlikely possibilities and assume that most relevant conditions stay the same. Consequently, their conclusions are defeasible, or withdrawable. Nonmonotonic logics represent this feature. Some select preferred models; others use default rules and may yield multiple extensions, meaning different coherent sets of consequences. AI also developed formalisms for action and change, including the situation calculus. These represent initial situations, actions, preconditions, effects, and goals. The frame problem asks how a system can represent persistence while still allowing actions to change what they should. The qualification problem concerns exceptions and possible failure, while the ramification problem concerns indirect effects. Benchmark scenarios, including the Yale Shooting Anomaly, are used to test whether a formalism gives the expected results. The broader field includes causal and spatial reasoning, reasoning about knowledge, taxonomies,18?
key_ideas: Logic-based AI tries to make reasoning about practical situations precise enough for computer programs, not merely to study small examples.
A knowledge representation component can store a general fact once and let many procedures use it. This can make systems easier to modify and better able to explain conclusions.
Classical logic is monotonic: if premises support a conclusion, adding more premises does not remove it. Everyday reasoning is often nonmonotonic because it depends on defaults and exceptions.
Planning requires reasoning about action, change, causes, goals, and the things that remain unchanged. The frame problem focuses on this last issue.
Several approaches compete or complement one another, including default logic, circumscription, modal approaches, preferred models, and causal theories.
Philosophical logic and AI overlap, but their methods and priorities differ. AI must consider algorithms, large data and rule collections, computational limits, and useful applications.
summaries.why_it_matters: Logic-based AI matters because intelligent systems need organized knowledge and dependable ways to revise conclusions. It also provides a meeting point for philosophy and computer science. Philosophical ideas help clarify concepts such as knowledge, causation, time, and practical reasoning, while AI forces those ideas to work in detailed, changing, and sometimes very large environments. The result is not one finished theory of common sense, but a set of tools and problems that deepen our understanding of reasoning.

important_terms.definition: A system of rules for telling which conclusions follow from information.
The field of computer science that builds programs able to perform tasks associated with intelligent behavior.
A structured store of facts, concepts, and relations that a reasoning system can use in different tasks.
Reasoning in which new information may defeat an earlier conclusion.
A tentative rule based on what normally happens, unless evidence blocks it.
A description of a possible state of affairs used to evaluate whether statements are true.
A formal description of how actions change situations, used in reasoning and planning.
The problem of explaining why most facts persist after an action without incorrectly preventing real changes.

questions_to_think_about: Why is a default useful even though it can sometimes lead to a wrong conclusion?
How might a program decide whether a new fact is a genuine exception?
Why can a simple rule about persistence create a surprising result in a longer action sequence?
What advantages might come from storing knowledge separately from the procedures that use it?
Should a logical theory be judged mainly by elegance, practical success, or both?
